newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-US Sept payrolls could signal neutral Fed.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-US Sept payrolls could signal neutral Fed.

text.p: The September U.S. employment report might persuade investors to bet on neutral Federal Reserve monetary policy for the next couple of months, economists said on Friday.
Although the economy created more than 200,000 new jobs each month from May through August, 26 economists in a Reuters survey projected, on average, that 166,000 new jobs were added in September.
At the same time, the unemployment rate rose slightly to 5.2 percent in September from 5.1 percent the month before, the experts forecast.

"The bond market is trying to figure out whether the Fed can wait longer after staying on hold at its last (policy) meeting," said Peter Kretzmer, an economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc. "A report like this would tend to argue, yes."
After central bank policymakers ended this week's meeting without raising interest rates, inflation doves quickly touted post-meeting data as evidence of the Fed's credibility:
durable goods orders fell 3.1 percent last month and weekly jobless claims breeched the 330,000-level for the first time in several weeks.
But both of those reports fluctuate widely.

The central bank's next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting is set for November 13, and many economists believe next Friday's jobs data will set the stage for another interest rate non-event.
"If we get a sanguine employment report, combined with (a weak September) retail sales report, then I think the Fed would stay on hold," said Kretzmer.
Economists calling for lower payrolls said a boomlet of teaching jobs boosted payrolls last month, while earlier start dates for the school year skewed the report's seasonal adjustments.

"There are a couple of factors that inflated August, but the same factors are going to deflate the September number a little," said Michael Strauss, executive vice president and chief economist at Yamaichi International (America) Inc.
Last month non-farm payrolls grew by 250,000 and the unemployment rate dipped to 5.1 percent.
"People are saying 30 (or) 40 thousand will have to come off that number" to account for the teacher bloat, said Astrid Adolfson, senior economist at MCM MoneyWatch Inc.
A drop of greater magnitude might hint at weakening of the labor market's underlying trend, some economists said. But most of the experts said the labor sector remains tight.
Strauss, for instance, forecast a payrolls number of 175,000, and he said anything over 125,000 would suggest job creation "above long-term (sustainable) employment growth."

"There is a good chance the (Treasury) market is going to try to view the number in a favorable light," said Strauss. "(But) there might be some disappointment if it's not significantly weaker than what we're talking about."

Besides payrolls and the unemployment rate, the economists in the Reuters survey projected average hourly earnings rose 0.2 percent to $11.89. And they forecast the average workweek expanded one-tenth of an hour to 34.5 hours.

Such small increases should not cause much concern for bond investors or others who fear wage inflation, said NationsBanc's Kretzmer. While hourly earnings have risen steadily in recent months, real earnings have grown by less than 1.0 percent in the past year, he said.
"I really don't think that's too out of line," said Kretzmer.
